notes.b: Mass movement is the downhill movement of soil and rock under gravity. People can make it happen more often and faster, or reduce it, depending on how they treat slopes.
points: Humans make mass movement more frequent and faster in three ways: by removing the vegetation that binds soil and absorbs water, by adding water or weight to slopes, and by removing support at the base of slopes.
Managing slopes can reduce the risk, because the same three factors can be reversed: keep vegetation, keep water out and keep the base supported.

Removing vegetation also exposes soil to rain splash (raindrops knocking soil particles loose), sheet wash (thin water flow over the whole surface), gullying (water cutting channels) and wind, which strip it away. Slopes then become prone to creep, slides and mudflows.
Answers may cover soil erosion as well as mass movement, provided the link to slopes and gravity is made.
notes.tip: A 30-mark question asks how humans interact with mass movement. For each human activity, say how it affects slope stability, give a named example with specific facts, and give management. Soil erosion is accepted only if you link it to slopes and gravity.

notes.h: Overgrazing: how it happens and its effects
notes.b: Overgrazing means keeping more animals on land than it can feed. It removes the plant cover that holds a slope together, so it is one of the three human activities the syllabus names.
points: Too many animals for the land's carrying capacity (the number it can support without damage) eat the vegetation down to the roots and trample the ground.
Hooves compact the soil and break the surface of peat, leaving bare patches.
Without roots, soil and peat lose cohesion (the way the particles stick together). Rain runs off the compacted surface or saturates the broken peat, so the ground is both weaker and wetter.
Sheet and gully erosion increase, soil creep (slow downhill movement of soil) speeds up as terracettes (small step-like ridges on a slope) deepen, and peat slides occur.
Sediment from the eroded slopes silts up rivers and damages fish spawning beds.
notes.tip: Keep overgrazing in its own answer, separate from overcropping and deforestation, so you can answer on any one of them. Do not claim overgrazing caused the Pollatomish landslides (2003): they were triggered by an intense storm.

notes.b: In Ireland, overgrazing occurred on the hill commonage of the west, where grazing land is shared. A payment system encouraged farmers to keep far more sheep than the hills could carry.
points: From the 1980s, EU (CAP) headage payments paid farmers per animal, so sheep numbers rose sharply on hill commonage (shared mountain grazing) in western Ireland, including Connemara, Co. Galway, and the mountains of Co. Mayo, Co. Donegal and Co. Kerry.
Overgrazing stripped heather and grass and exposed and eroded blanket peat (a thick layer of peat covering upland ground). Silt then entered rivers, harming salmon and trout spawning grounds.
Response 1: payments were changed from per-head to per-area, so farmers no longer gained by adding animals.
Response 2: Commonage Framework Plans, from the early 2000s, set lower stocking rates (fewer animals per area).
Response 3: REPS (the Rural Environment Protection Scheme, introduced in 1994) paid farmers to farm in environmentally friendly ways.
notes.tip: Use specific facts: the cause (headage payments from the 1980s), the places, the effects on peat and rivers, and the responses.

notes.b: Each management method tackles the cause of overgrazing: too many animals, or animals staying too long in one place.
points: Destocking: reducing the number of animals to the land's carrying capacity, so the vegetation is no longer eaten down to the roots.
Rotational grazing, moving animals between areas so that vegetation can recover.
Fencing off degraded ground to let vegetation recover, because the roots can then bind the soil again.

notes.h: Overcropping: how it happens and its effects
notes.b: Overcropping means growing crops on the same land too intensively, so the soil is worn out. Weak, bare soil is then easily carried away.
points: The same land is cropped year after year without fallow periods (rest years with no crop) or fertiliser. Soil nutrients and organic matter are used up, and soil structure breaks down.
Crops grow poorly, the ground is left bare between harvests, and marginal (poor-quality) and sloping land is ploughed.
Loose, dry, structureless soil is washed downslope by rain or blown away by wind, forming rills (tiny channels) and gullies (larger, deeper channels).
On slopes, ploughing up and down the slope channels water and soil downhill, because the furrows act like drains.
notes.tip: Keep overcropping as its own answer. For the Dust Bowl, focus on overcropping as the human cause.

notes.h: Overcropping case study: the Dust Bowl
notes.b: The Dust Bowl shows how ploughing up natural cover and then meeting a drought can strip a whole region of its soil.
points: On the Great Plains of the USA, including Oklahoma and Kansas, natural grassland was ploughed up for wheat in the 1930s.
Severe drought then left bare, dry soil, which wind erosion removed in huge dust storms, because there were no grass roots to hold it.
Many farming families were forced to leave, because the land could no longer grow crops.

The US Soil Conservation Service was set up in 1935. Shelter belts of trees (rows of trees that break the wind), contour ploughing (ploughing along the slope) and crop rotation (changing the crop grown each year) were promoted.
notes.tip: Link the Dust Bowl to wind erosion, but make overcropping (ploughing up the grassland) the human cause.

notes.b: The Sahel is an international example in which overgrazing and overcropping act together, with fuelwood cutting added.
points: The Sahel is the semi-arid (very dry) belt along the southern edge of the Sahara.
Population growth led to more cattle, goats and sheep concentrated around wells and boreholes, so the land around the water was grazed bare.
Population growth also led to shorter fallow periods and more cash crops (crops grown to sell), which is overcropping, and to more fuelwood cutting.
With droughts, notably in the 1970s and 1980s, the bare soil was eroded by wind and by the heavy rain of the short wet season. This process is called desertification (land turning into desert).

notes.b: Management either keeps the soil fed and covered, or stops water and wind from carrying it away.
points: Crop rotation and fallow periods, so that soil nutrients recover.
Contour ploughing, ploughing along the slope rather than up and down it, so furrows hold water instead of channelling it downhill.
Strip cropping (growing crops in alternate strips), terracing of steep slopes (cutting level steps into them), and shelter belts against wind.
Mulching (covering the soil with plant material) and cover crops keep the soil covered between harvests.
Example: the rice terraces of Banaue, Luzon, Philippines, show terracing of steep slopes that is over 2,000 years old.

notes.h: Deforestation: how it happens and its effects
notes.b: Deforestation is the clearing of forest. Trees hold a slope together and manage the water that falls on it, so removing them makes slopes much less stable.
points: Trees are removed for farmland, timber, fuelwood, roads and building, so forest is replaced by bare or thinly covered ground.

Tree roots bind soil and anchor it to bedrock. The canopy breaks the force of rain, and trees take up water (interception, where leaves catch rain, and transpiration, where plants release water vapour).
Without trees, more rain reaches and saturates the soil. Roots rot and no longer hold the slope.
Landslides and mudflows become more frequent, especially in heavy tropical rain. More sediment and faster run-off reach rivers.
notes.tip: Keep deforestation as its own answer with how it affects slope stability, named examples with facts, and management. Do not say Himalayan deforestation causes Bangladesh's floods, as the link is disputed, and do not name a Nepal example.

notes.h: Deforestation case studies: Haiti and Central America
notes.b: Two international examples show how deforested slopes turn heavy rain into deadly floods and mudflows.
points: Haiti has lost almost all its natural forest, mainly for farmland and charcoal. Neighbouring Dominican Republic has far more forest cover.
In September 2004 Tropical Storm Jeanne caused floods and mudslides off the bare hills around Gonaïves, killing about 3,000 people.
Hurricane Mitch, October 1998: torrential rain over Honduras and Nicaragua caused floods and landslides, made worse by deforested slopes. About 11,000 people were killed.
A mudflow from the Casita volcano, Nicaragua, buried villages during Hurricane Mitch.

notes.b: Ireland has little woodland left after centuries of clearance, and modern forestry can still destabilise upland slopes.
points: Historic forest clearance left Ireland with very little woodland. About 1% of Ireland was forested around 1900.
Forest cover is now about 11%, so it has risen since 1900, mostly in conifer plantations.
Clear-felling (cutting down all the trees in an area at once) of conifer plantations on upland peat, and building forestry and wind-farm roads, can destabilise peat slopes.

notes.b: These methods keep tree roots and canopy in place on the slopes that need them most.
points: Afforestation (planting trees where there were none) and reforestation (replanting where trees were cut) of steep slopes, so roots bind the soil again.
Buffer strips of trees beside rivers, so that roots hold the banks and trap sediment.
Selective felling (removing only some trees) instead of clear-felling, and restricting felling on steep or peaty slopes.

notes.h: Construction on peat: Derrybrien and Meenbog
notes.b: Building on upland blanket bog can cause peat slides, because the work disturbs a wet, weak slope. Exams accept this as a human cause of mass movement.
points: Wind farms and roads on upland blanket bog involve excavation, dumping of spoil (waste material dug out) on the bog surface and interference with drainage.

Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway, 16 October 2003: during construction of a wind farm on a forested blanket-bog hillside, a peat slide of about 450,000 cubic metres moved into the Owendalulleegh River, killing large numbers of fish.

In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland, a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day, because no proper environmental impact assessment (a study of likely damage before building) had been carried out.

Meenbog wind farm, near Ballybofey, Co. Donegal, November 2020: a peat slide during construction flowed into the Mourne Beg River and crossed into Northern Ireland, polluting a river system important for salmon.
notes.tip: For a news article on a bog burst at a wind farm, give the county, the cause (construction activity) and the impacts (river pollution, fish kills). Derrybrien is in Co. Galway (Slieve Aughty), not Co. Clare. Meenbog is in Co. Donegal. Do not use the Cummeragh Mountain bogburst.

notes.h: Other human causes: cuttings, weight, water and spoil
notes.b: Anything that steepens a slope, loads it, wets it or removes its support raises the risk of mass movement.
points: Road and rail cuttings steepen slopes or remove support at their base, so the slope above is left unsupported.
Building weight on top of a slope adds to the downslope force.
Leaking pipes, drainage and irrigation saturate slopes, because extra water adds weight and reduces friction between particles.
Reservoirs saturate valley sides. Vajont is the example.
Mining spoil heaps (piles of waste rock) are unstable. Aberfan is the example.
notes.tip: Do not claim that urban construction in Dublin or Cork causes landslides: no checked Irish urban example exists.

notes.b: Slope risk can be cut by physically strengthening slopes, and by planning so that people avoid or are warned about the danger.
points: Slope engineering: retaining walls, gabions (wire cages of stones), rock bolts, wire netting and rock-catch fences on cliffs, all of which hold or catch loose material.
Regrading slopes to a gentler angle, and drainage pipes to lower the water content.
Planning: hazard mapping, avoiding building on unstable slopes, and environmental impact assessments before building on peat.
Monitoring and warning systems, so that people can leave before a slope fails.

keyTerms.definition: The number of animals an area of land can support without its vegetation being damaged.
Grazing by too many animals, which eats vegetation down to the roots and compacts the soil.
Cropping the same land year after year without fallow periods or fertiliser, so the soil structure breaks down.
A period when land is left unplanted to let its nutrients and structure recover.
Ploughing along the slope rather than up and down it, to slow the flow of water and soil.
The degradation of semi-arid land into desert-like conditions through overuse, drought and erosion.
The removal of trees, which loses the roots that bind soil and the canopy that intercepts rain.
Cutting down all the trees in an area at once.
A wire cage filled with stones, used to retain a slope.
Waterlogged peat that covers upland slopes and can burst or slide when saturated.

factCards.term: Human activity: three ways it makes mass movement more frequent
factCards.definition: Removing the vegetation that binds soil and absorbs water; adding water or weight to slopes; removing the support at the base of slopes. Bare soil is also stripped by rain splash, sheet wash, gullying and wind.

factCards.term: Overgrazing: how it leads to soil erosion and mass movement
factCards.definition: Too many animals for the carrying capacity eat vegetation to the roots and trample the ground, compacting soil and breaking the peat; without roots, soil and peat lose cohesion, rain runs off or saturates the peat, creep speeds up and peat slides occur.

factCards.term: Western Irish commonage: how overgrazing happened and its effects
factCards.definition: From the 1980s, EU (CAP) headage payments paid per animal, so sheep numbers rose sharply on western hill commonage (Connemara; the Mayo, Donegal and Kerry mountains). Heather and grass were stripped, peat eroded and silt hurt salmon and trout spawning grounds.

factCards.term: Overgrazing: how it has been managed, with Irish measures
factCards.definition: Payments changed from per-head to per-area; Commonage Framework Plans (from the early 2000s) set lower stocking rates; REPS, introduced in 1994, paid farmers to farm in environmentally friendly ways. Also destocking, rotational grazing and fencing.

factCards.term: The Sahel: how overgrazing and overcropping led to desertification
factCards.definition: Population growth brought more cattle, goats and sheep around wells and boreholes, shorter fallow periods, more cash crops and more fuelwood cutting; in droughts, notably in the 1970s and 1980s, wind and the short wet season's heavy rain eroded the bare soil.

factCards.term: Overcropping: how it leads to soil erosion on slopes
factCards.definition: Cropping land every year without fallow or fertiliser uses up nutrients, so soil structure breaks down and ground lies bare; loose, dry soil is washed downslope into rills and gullies or blown away; ploughing up and down slopes channels water and soil down.

factCards.term: Dust Bowl, 1930s: how overcropping caused it and its effects
factCards.definition: On the Great Plains of the USA, including Oklahoma and Kansas, natural grassland was ploughed up for wheat; severe drought then left bare, dry soil that strong winds blew away in huge dust storms; many farming families were forced to leave.

factCards.term: Dust Bowl: how the USA responded
factCards.definition: The US Soil Conservation Service was set up in 1935, and shelter belts of trees, contour ploughing and crop rotation were promoted.

factCards.term: Overcropping: five management methods, with an example
factCards.definition: Crop rotation; fallow periods; contour ploughing along the slope, not up and down; strip cropping; terracing of steep slopes, e.g. the rice terraces of Banaue, Luzon, Philippines, over 2,000 years old.

factCards.term: Deforestation: how it increases landslides and mudflows
factCards.definition: Roots bind soil to bedrock, the canopy breaks the force of rain, and trees take up water. Without trees, more rain reaches and saturates the soil and rotting roots no longer hold the slope, so landslides and mudflows become more frequent.

factCards.term: Haiti, 2004: how deforestation worsened a disaster

factCards.term: Ireland's forests: two figures and a modern risk to peat slopes
factCards.definition: About 1% of Ireland was forested around 1900; forest cover is now about 11%, mostly conifer plantations. Clear-felling plantations on upland peat, and building forestry and wind-farm roads, can destabilise peat slopes.

factCards.term: Deforestation: four ways to manage its effect on slopes
factCards.definition: Afforestation and reforestation of steep slopes; buffer strips of trees beside rivers; selective felling instead of clear-felling; restricting felling on steep or peaty slopes.

On 16 October 2003, during construction of a wind farm on a forested blanket-bog hillside in the Slieve Aughty Mountains, about 450,000 cubic metres of peat slid down the slope into the Owendalulleegh River, killing large numbers of fish.

factCards.term: Derrybrien: why the EU fined Ireland
factCards.definition: In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day, because no proper environmental impact assessment had been carried out for the wind farm.

In November 2020 a peat slide during construction of the Meenbog wind farm, near Ballybofey, flowed into the Mourne Beg River and crossed into Northern Ireland, polluting a river system important for salmon.

factCards.term: Other human causes of mass movement: name five
factCards.definition: Road and rail cuttings that steepen slopes or remove their support; buildings adding weight at the top of slopes; leaking pipes, drainage and irrigation saturating slopes; reservoirs saturating valley sides (Vajont); unstable mining spoil heaps (Aberfan).

factCards.term: Reducing the risk of mass movement: engineering and planning
factCards.definition: Engineering: retaining walls, gabions, rock bolts, netting and rock-catch fences, regrading slopes, drainage pipes. Planning: hazard mapping, avoiding unstable slopes, environmental impact assessments before building on peat, monitoring and warning systems.

questions.prompt: Examine how human activities can impact on mass movement processes, with reference to overgrazing, overcropping and deforestation.
questions.model: Overgrazing: too many animals strip vegetation and compact the soil, so roots no longer bind it and rain saturates or runs off it. Peat slides and faster creep follow. Example: sheep overgrazing on western Irish commonage after the headage payments of the 1980s. Management: destocking, rotational grazing and fencing. Overcropping: repeated cropping without fallow exhausts soil structure and leaves ground bare; rain and wind remove loose soil and rills and gullies form. Example: the Dust Bowl of the 1930s on the Great Plains of the USA. Management: crop rotation, fallow periods, contour ploughing and shelter belts. Deforestation: roots and canopy are removed, so more rain saturates the soil and roots rot. Landslides and mudflows become more frequent. Example: Hurricane Mitch, 1998, in Honduras and Nicaragua, or Haiti, 2004. Management: reforestation of steep slopes, buffer strips and selective felling.

questions.prompt: Examine how humans interact with mass movement processes, with reference to Irish examples.
questions.model: Overgrazing of western Irish commonage after the headage payments of the 1980s stripped vegetation, exposed blanket peat and increased peat slides; REPS and Commonage Framework Plans later reduced stocking. Derrybrien, Co. Galway, 2003: wind-farm construction on forested blanket bog caused a peat slide of about 450,000 cubic metres into the Owendalulleegh River and killed large numbers of fish; the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland in 2019 for lacking an environmental impact assessment. Meenbog, Co. Donegal, 2020: a construction-related peat slide polluted a river system important for salmon. Forestry on upland peat: clear-felling and forestry roads can destabilise peat slopes; about 11% of Ireland is now forested, mostly conifer plantations. Management: environmental impact assessments before building on peat, selective felling, and restricting felling on peaty slopes.

questions.prompt: Explain how deforestation can increase mass movement.
questions.model: Tree roots bind soil and anchor it to bedrock, so without them the soil loses cohesion. The canopy breaks the force of rain and trees take up water through interception and transpiration; without trees, more rain reaches and saturates the soil. Roots rot and no longer hold the slope. Landslides and mudflows become more frequent, especially in heavy tropical rain, and more sediment and run-off reach rivers. Example: Hurricane Mitch, October 1998, over Honduras and Nicaragua, where floods and landslides were made worse by deforested slopes, and a mudflow from the Casita volcano buried villages. Example: Haiti, where Tropical Storm Jeanne in September 2004 caused mudslides off bare hills around Gonaïves. Reforestation of steep slopes and buffer strips of trees beside rivers reduce the risk.
